meta.title: Who really said "Ignorance of each other is what has made unity impossible in the past. Therefore we need enlightenment. We need more light about each other. Light creates understanding, understanding creates love, love creates patience, and patience creates unity"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Traced to one book — a Malcolm X anthology, p. 304 — but no speech, letter or date has ever been named. Verdict: attributed, not verified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Ignorance of each other is what has made unity impossible in the past. Therefore we need enlightenment. We need more light about each other. Light creates understanding, understanding creates love, love creates patience, and patience creates unity'?
meta.ogDescription: The one real citation runs to Malcolm X: The Man and His Times, p. 304. No speech, no letter, no date — and everywhere else it circulates with no source at all.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1925–1965 · Muslim minister and Black nationalist leader
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Malcolm X, and the one real citation trail leads somewhere serious: Wikiquote ↗ lists the full passage with a page reference to Malcolm X: The Man and His Times, edited by John Henrik Clarke (Africa World Press, 1990), p. 304. But no speech, letter or interview behind it has ever been named — Wikiquote files the line under “Date unverified,” and everywhere else it travels with no source at all.

source.excerpt: Ignorance of each other is what has made unity impossible in the past. Therefore we need enlightenment. We need more light about each other. Light creates understanding, understanding creates love, love creates patience, and patience creates unity. Once we have more knowledge (light) about each other, we will stop condemning each other and a United front will be brought about.
trail: Wikiquote’s Malcolm X page ↗ carries the full passage inside its Quotes section, in a subsection headed “Date unverified,” with a page reference to Malcolm X: The Man and His Times, edited by John Henrik Clarke and published by Africa World Press in 1990, p. 304.
A search inside that volume on Google Books ↗ returns a page match for the quote’s closing words — but the book is snippet-view only, so no reader can see what document p. 304 belongs to.
A 1969 printing of the anthology is scanned at the Internet Archive ↗, but the item is access-restricted, so its full text is not publicly searchable and the occasion behind p. 304 stays unconfirmed.
Quote Investigator ↗ has never taken the quotation up — a site search for “patience creates unity” returns nothing — so there is no specialist tracing to defer to here.
source.excerptNote: The closing sentence — almost always dropped when the line is shared — is the part that anchors it. A search inside the volume on Google Books ↗ reports a page match for “we will stop condemning each other” and for “a United front will be brought about,” which is independent confirmation that the passage really is in the book, even though the page itself cannot be read.

source.rightsHolder: The estate of Malcolm X (commercially represented by CMG Worldwide); the cited collection is published by Africa World Press.
source.rightsNote: Whatever Malcolm X said or wrote here, he said it in the 1960s, and the earliest printing anyone can point to is a 1969 anthology — both far too recent for the US public domain. The official Malcolm X site ↗ carries a standing copyright notice and states that CMG Worldwide represents him, so treat the wording as in copyright: quote it briefly, with attribution.

author.name: Malcolm X
author.heading: Who was Malcolm X?
author.metaLine: 1925–1965 · Muslim minister and Black nationalist leader
author.bio: Born Malcolm Little in Omaha, Nebraska on 19 May 1925, he became the Nation of Islam’s best-known national spokesman before leaving the movement in 1964 and founding Muslim Mosque, Inc. and the Organization of Afro-American Unity. He was assassinated in New York City on 21 February 1965. Much of his speaking was extemporaneous and only patchily transcribed at the time — which is precisely why passages like this one can circulate for decades documented in a book yet still unattached to any occasion.

misattribution.heading: The problem isn't the wrong name — it's no source
misattribution.intro: Nobody credible pins this passage on a different person. The failure is the opposite one: it travels almost everywhere with no citation whatsoever, which is how a genuine-looking piece of Malcolm X material ends up impossible to check.

items.why: The Goodreads entry ↗ reproduces the full passage under Malcolm X’s name with no work, date or occasion attached — and it is that citation-free version, not the book reference, that the rest of the web copies.

A shorter cut beginning “We need more light about each other” circulates as a separate quotation ↗, dropping both the opening sentence about ignorance and the closing one about a united front — which is where the passage’s political point actually lives.
A 2020 Al Jazeera opinion piece ↗ quotes the passage in full and gives no source, date or publication for it — a fair measure of how far the line moves even in careful company.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest position: the passage is documented in a real book of Malcolm X material — Wikiquote ↗ cites Malcolm X: The Man and His Times, p. 304 — but until someone names the speech, letter or interview behind it, “attributed” is as far as the evidence goes.

context.heading: Why the missing source matters here
lead: Unity was Malcolm X’s late preoccupation. In 1964 he left the Nation of Islam and founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity ↗, and at its founding rally ↗ he pressed for a common front among Black Americans — freedom, justice and equality “by any means necessary.” The thinking in this passage sits squarely in that stretch of his life.

But sounding like someone is not evidence, and that is exactly the trap with a name this heavily quoted. The passage is not in the text of that founding-rally speech, and it is not among the sourced Autobiography or Malcolm X Speaks extracts on Wikiquote ↗, where it sits in a section of its own headed “Date unverified.” Its single citation is a page number in an anthology published in 1969, four years after his death. That is enough to take the line seriously and not enough to call it verified.
detailsBody: Page 304 of Malcolm X: The Man and His Times is the whole ballgame. The volume is snippet-view only on Google Books ↗ and lending-restricted on the Internet Archive ↗, so the surrounding text cannot be read online. A library copy would show at a stroke whether p. 304 falls inside a Malcolm X document the editors reprinted — a speech, a letter, an interview — or inside a contributor’s essay quoting him.
Until that check is made, the honest way to share it is the full passage with the book citation attached, rather than the trimmed inspirational cut that dominates social media.
context.pull: Documented in a book. Undocumented in a moment.
